title: Risk categories in three providers' safety frameworks

opening.headline: Read the risk classification of the safety framework published by the provider, and learn how to connect it with the organization's risk management practices.
body: OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind each release their own safety frameworks. OpenAI presents the Preparedness Framework, Anthropic introduces the Responsible Scaling Policy, and Google DeepMind launches the Frontier Safety Framework. The terminology for risks and stages varies across each document.

Meanwhile, the risk register of an organization lists operational risks such as information leakage, incorrect responses, and regulatory violations. It is difficult to assess how a provider's changes impact our operational risks if the two lists are not clearly aligned. In this course, we examine the structure and risk domains of three frameworks and learn through examples how to align them with an organization's risk management practices.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: This can describe the risk areas of three company safety frameworks.
Can analyze the provider's risk classification in relation to the organization's risk management and response.

screens.title: How does the provider's risk classification align with our risk management?
screens.lead:
First, read the point that the risk classification from the provider and the organization's risk register are written in different languages.

As of 2026-10, RSP v3.4 is a policy that jointly reads risk mitigation measures, Frontier Safety Roadmap, and Risk Reports. Previous versions that described only the ASL stage do not conclusively define all current training and deployment conditions.

Google DeepMind FSF added traceability level (TCL) in certain areas starting from April 17, 2026, version 3.1. Do not read this solely as a CCL system—instead, distinguish between the two levels of purpose and applicable scope.

visual.alt: Diagram connecting the three provider frameworks on the left with the organizational risk matrix on the right via question marks.

paragraphs: The three providers each publish their own safety frameworks. OpenAI releases the Preparedness Framework, Anthropic publishes the Responsible Scaling Policy, and Google DeepMind presents the Frontier Safety Framework. All of these documents describe how they measure and mitigate severe risks that cutting-edge AI models might pose.
Each document uses different terms for risk and its levels. Some documents refer to tracking categories and capability levels, others to AI Safety Levels, and yet others to core capability levels.

On the other hand, the risk catalog for an organization lists risks such as information leakage, incorrect responses, and regulatory violations that occur in daily operations. Without a clear alignment between these two lists, it is difficult to determine which of our risks are affected when the provider changes its policies. This course's question is: how should the provider's risk classification be connected to the organization's risk management?

callout.label: Note
callout.text: The provider's framework addresses frontline capabilities that could lead to severe damage, while the organization's risk appetite manages the risks arising from our operations. The two are distinct in scope.

screens.outro: First, let us recall our experience reading these documents.

screens.title: Have you ever read about the provider's security framework?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: If you reviewed the provider's safety framework, which aspect—risk areas or mitigation steps—remains most memorable to you?
items.answer: Two roles are different. The risk domain addresses what is managed, while the mitigation steps address what safety mechanisms are required as risk increases. When connecting to an organization's risk management, both must be read.

items.prompt: Is there an item in our risk management documentation that references the provider's policies?
items.answer: If there are no items being referenced, it means there is no pathway through which the provider's policy changes are communicated to risk management. In this course, provider policies are connected at three points: as an input to model selection, as a constraint on workflow design, and as a signal for reevaluation.

items.prompt: Who determines the impact when the provider's policy changes?
items.answer: If no owner is assigned, change notifications are not read and are simply overlooked. By predefining how to read notifications and specifying owners, change reviews become shorter and more consistent.

screens.outro: Now I will check each framework's structure and terminology one by one.

screens.title: The structure and terminology of the three frameworks
screens.lead: When you select a card, it flips over to show an explanation. To move to the next card, select the right-arrow.

cards.back: A framework for tracking and preparing against frontline capabilities that could cause severe damage. Tracking categories include bioweapons, chemical weapons, and cyber security, while areas still below established standards are designated as research categories. Capability levels are classified as High and Critical.

The Safety Advisory Group (SAG), a forum of safety responsibility officers from various departments, reviews and provides recommendations on whether safety mechanisms adequately mitigate risks. Recommendations can range from approval to additional evaluations or requests for enhanced protections, with final decisions made by OpenAI's executive leadership. Systems with high capability must have safety mechanisms in place prior to deployment.

As of 2026-10, RSP v3.4 is a policy that reads together Risk Mitigation Measures, Frontier Safety Roadmap, and Risk Reports. Descriptions of past ASL stages do not determine all current training and deployment conditions.

Define the critical capability level (CCL), detect whether that level is achieved during the model lifecycle, and implement mitigation plans if reached. Conduct a safety review prior to external release when that level is attained.

cards.front: Common structure of the three frameworks
cards.back: The question of linking risk assessment and response to deployment decisions is common. However, it is not valid to assume that measures have the same level of enforceability, that the reviewing body is the same, or that the public procedure is identical.

The absence of an item with the same name does not mean there is no risk; therefore, the original classification and applicable scope must be verified separately.

screens.outro: Having reviewed the risk area, let's now examine how to respond to it within the organization's risk management.

screens.title: Align supplier risk classification with organizational risk management
screens.lead: Select an item to expand, and verify the three points of intersection between the provider's categorization and the organization's risk management.

items.title: First, acknowledge that the scope is different.
items.body: The provider's classification addresses the extreme risks encountered throughout model development. Organizational risk management deals with risks that may arise in our work. Therefore, we do not simply adopt the names verbatim, but establish connection points to link them appropriately.

items.title: Contact 1: Input for model selection
items.body: When a provider releases a model, we use the capability evaluation results and safety measures they publicly disclose as inputs for our model selection. OpenAI publicly releases preparedness results each time it launches a new frontier model.

items.title: Point 2: Constraints of task design
items.body: Access restrictions and usage conditions are recorded as constraints of workflow design. Distinguish between corporate policy requirements and objectives, and verify the actual measures applied and the scope of provision within the respective model.

items.title: Point 3: Signal for Reevaluation
items.body: This signals a need to review our risk lead when the framework changes. OpenAI documents refer to the framework as a living document and states that it will be continuously updated. Therefore, the response matrix is periodically updated as well.

screens.outro: Now, let's illustrate the impact of access restrictions on work plans through an example.

screens.title: Commentary: Functions and work plans with restricted access
screens.lead: The instructor breaks down the process that involves access restrictions reaching the work plan step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: case
steps.body: This is a hypothetical scenario. Our team planned a service that relies on the capabilities of a certain large language model, but let's assume the provider has restricted the public availability of that model. Can we proceed with the original plan?

steps.title: Why the restrictions exist is understood.
steps.body: OpenAI explains that it will not deploy systems with high capabilities until safety measures have sufficiently reduced risks. Anthropic must independently verify the current RSP and risk assessment report, which may result in limited public availability or functionality.

steps.title: Find the model that the planned functionality depends on
steps.body: Check the service list to determine which planned features depend on a specific model. Without knowing the dependencies, you cannot understand which plans are affected.

steps.title: Verifies access conditions and determines whether they are satisfied.
steps.body: Review the usage conditions outlined by the provider and determine whether our organization meets those conditions. If separate procedures are required to verify condition fulfillment, include the time taken by those procedures in the schedule.

steps.title: If not satisfied, adjust the scope.
steps.body: If conditions are not met, adjust the functionality scope to an unconstrained alternative model. While functionality may be reduced, certain guarantees can still be upheld.

steps.title: result
steps.body: The vendor's risk classification has manifested as a constraint determining our scope and functional boundaries. Recording this constraint in the work design documentation will help avoid repeating the same mistakes in future plans.

screens.outro: Now we will look at the response when the provider framework is updated.

screens.title: Explanation: Reflect the provider framework change in the risk register
screens.lead: The provider breaks down the framework update process step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed.

steps.title: case
steps.body: Suppose the provider updated the framework to change the risk categories and safety measures. In reality, Google DeepMind added a core capability level for handling harmful manipulations in version 3 and expanded the scope of risks related to misalignment.

steps.title: Organizes the change content by risk areas
steps.body: Divide changes by risk areas. Separate newly introduced categories, changed levels, and safety requirements. This organization makes it easier to identify which aspects of the organization are involved.

steps.title: Find the relevant items from the organizational risk matrix.
steps.body: The system searches for relevant items in the risk matrix based on the service using this model and the type of data being handled. For example, if the service involves directly interacting with users through speech, it may relate to changes associated with manipulation, such as incorrect responses or loss of trust.

steps.title: Items affected are re-evaluated.
steps.body: Items where the risk assessment changes are reviewed by the responsible party, and actions taken are documented.

steps.title: Items unaffected are left with a note.
steps.body: We leave a rationale stating no impact, even for items judged to have no effect. Having a rationale allows us to avoid re-evaluating from scratch when reviewing the same change later.

steps.title: result
steps.body: If a standardized process for reviewing provider documentation is established, the change review becomes short and consistent. This review process itself becomes part of risk management.

screens.outro: Finally, let me summarize three key points.

screens.title: The Intersection of Supplier Risk Classification and Organizational Risk Management
screens.lead: We summarize the contact points discussed in this class in order.

paragraphs: **Input**: The provider's capability assessment and safety measures serve as input for our model selection. The evaluation results released alongside the launch are read as the basis for choosing the model.

**Constraints**: Access restrictions and usage policies are constraints of workflow design. These constraints are expressed in terms of schedules and functional scope and are recorded in the workflow design documentation.

**Signal**: A framework change signals a need to reevaluate the risk domains. Organize the changes by risk area, identify related items, and reevaluate them; if there is no impact, document the rationale. The structures of the three companies are alike in that they assess capability and require safety mechanisms, so presenting them in a table eliminates confusion due to differences in naming.

callout.label: Core
callout.text: The provider's risk classification is input to organizational risk management.

checks.explain: All three companies assess capability levels and require appropriate safety measures, but their terminology and judgment frameworks differ.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes. I have accurately connected the terminology from the three companies.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Some pairs do not match. Think about the capability level terminology used by each company.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded or graded.
checks.q: The provider has updated its security framework, changing the risk categories and safety measures. What is the most appropriate response from an organizational risk management perspective?
options: This is internal documentation of the provider and is therefore unrelated to the organization's risk profile.
Organizes changes by risk areas and reviews the risk exposure items for services using the corresponding model.
Changes the name of all organization risk header items to the provider's new risk name.
Immediately discontinue usage of all models provided by the respective provider
checks.explain: Framework changes signal the need for a reassessment of risk exposure. Items affected are reviewed by the responsible party, while those unaffected shall document the rationale.

wrong.0: The provider's capability assessment and usage policy serve as inputs and constraints for model selection and workflow design.
wrong.2: Categorizing providers as such does not make sense because renaming it directly to reflect the extreme risks involved in model development fails to account for the organization's risks arising from operations.
wrong.3: Changes are a signal for review, not a basis for discontinuation, and the impact must be assessed first.

checks.correctFeedback: Yes. Changes are a signal for reevaluation.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Think again. Change does not mean deprecation or name alteration.

glossary.def: This is a framework for tracking and preparing against capabilities at the front lines that could lead to severe damage for OpenAI.
This is Anthropic's risk governance policy. Please read the current version, distinguishing between actions, objectives, and public reports.
Google DeepMind provides a framework that defines core capability levels (CCL) to assess and mitigate risks.
These are fields such as biology, chemistry, cybersecurity, and AI self-improvement, where frameworks are treated as the managed objects.
This is a control by the provider that limits the scope of public availability and usage conditions for a specific model or feature. This course examines this scenario as a hypothetical example.

misconceptions.myth: The provider's framework is unrelated to our organization.
misconceptions.fact: Our plan is constrained by model selection and access conditions. If the provider restricts public scope or usage conditions, it will result in limitations on schedule and functional scope.

misconceptions.myth: If the risk names of the three companies differ, their management targets also differ.
misconceptions.fact: The areas overlap. Although they have different names—such as biotechnology, chemical research, cybersecurity, and AI R&D—they address the same domain and are thus mapped and read in a table format.

misconceptions.myth: The framework is read once and done.
misconceptions.fact: The document is updated, so the corresponding table should also be periodically updated. Changes are a signal for reevaluation of the risk register.

closing.lead: This summarizes the core content of the class.
points: The provider's risk classification is input to organizational risk management.
The three frameworks have a structure that measures capability and requires safety mechanisms.
Access restrictions are recorded as constraints of the work plan.
